Module 6 — Species Interactions

Snapshot Brasil camera-trap analysis pipeline

1 What this module does

Modules 3–5 asked where each species lives. This module asks a harder question: does one species’ abundance depend on another’s? That is the difference between a map of co-occurrence and a claim about interaction — competition, predation, facilitation.

The module makes three moves:

  1. Why occupancy (co-occurrence) models are the wrong tool for inferring interactions, and what the alternative is.
  2. Fit an abundance-mediated interaction model for a focused set of driver-responder pairs, at the spatial resolution the data can actually support.
  3. Build two community-level interaction networks — one from the abundance model, one from GJAM’s residual co-occurrence — and read them together.

2 Why not occupancy models for interactions?

The most common way ecologists have tried to infer species interactions from camera-trap data is a multi-species occupancy model: fit occupancy for two species jointly and look at whether one species’ presence changes the other’s estimated occupancy probability, after habitat is accounted for. It is tempting because it uses exactly the same data already in hand — no separate model, no extra fieldwork.

It is also, on the current evidence, an unreliable way to detect interactions.

Sample size. Twining & Kellner (2026, Methods in Ecology and Evolution 17:456-479, doi: 10.1111/2041-210x.70210) ran a simulation study asking when hierarchical co-occurrence models can reliably recover a real two-species interaction. Their headline finding: datasets need more than 500 sites for two-species interactions to avoid a type M (magnitude) error — a confidently wrong size of effect — and they report that many previously published studies did not meet this minimum.

Bias, not just noise. The same paper identifies a more fundamental problem: even with enough sites, model misspecification — a shared habitat covariate or a third interacting species left out of the model — can produce a type S (sign) error: a confidently wrong direction, concluding avoidance when the truth is attraction, or vice versa. Both failure modes share a common mechanism, omitted-variable bias, the same problem that haunts ordinary linear regression; it does not go away with more data, only with the right covariates, which are rarely all known in advance. A related simulation study, Cowans, Bigata & Sutherland (2025, Ecology 106:e70175), independently confirms the sensitivity of co-occurrence inference to sample size and detection probability: bias in the interaction parameter is high below 100–1,000 sites depending on detection probability and interaction strength, and even at nearly 3,000 sites a weak co-occurrence signal is never consistently detected.

ImportantWhat this means for this module

Testing all 44×43 possible species pairs with an occupancy-style co-occurrence model would be both a multiple-testing fishing expedition and, per the above, statistically unreliable even before the multiple-testing problem is considered. This module instead uses an abundance-mediated approach — an N-mixture model where one species’ estimated abundance enters as a covariate in another’s abundance model — on a small, hypothesis-driven set of pairs, following the modeling approach of Amir, Sovie & Luskin (2022, Ecology and Evolution, doi: 10.1002/ece3.9627) and the sample-size-aware precedent of Twining (2025).

3 Which pairs, and why

Following the papers’ advice above, a focused set of pairs is tested rather than every possible combination:

  • 12 a-priori pairs — hypotheses from natural history: apex predators and their large prey (Jaguar → peccaries, tapir), mesopredator suppression (Jaguar/Puma → Ocelot → smaller cats), and competing frugivore/rodent guilds (agoutis, acouchi, paca).
  • 8 GJAM-flagged pairs — the strongest residual co-occurrences from the Module 4 joint model (association not explained by shared habitat), promoted to a formal abundance test.
  • 10 dog-driven pairs — domestic dog abundance as the driver, against a set of native species plausibly affected by dogs as a disturbance/competitor, since dogs are a human-associated species outside the a-priori and GJAM-flagged sets above.

4 Array-level results: the abundance-mediated network

The camera-level fits above (12 a-priori + 8 GJAM-flagged pairs) work at the ~1,100 individual camera stations. But for rare, wide-ranging species — jaguar especially — a single camera rarely records more than one detection per survey window, so the abundance signal at that unit is thin. The methodological precedent this pipeline follows — Twining’s and Amir & Luskin’s co-abundance frameworks — both fit this class of model on spatial units coarser than a single camera, sized closer to the study species’ home range. Module 5 already defines exactly such a unit: the 60-array partition. All 30 pairs (the 20 original camera-level pairs plus 10 dog-driven pairs) were refit at the array level, aggregating detections within each array for each 7-day window, using the reduced 6-covariate ARRAY_SET (forest, savanna, native vegetation, temperature, precipitation, distance to road) rather than the 11-covariate CAMERA_SET, since several camera-level-only covariates are not reliably estimated at the array’s coarser footprint.

#> Array-level pairs converged: 28 of 30

28 of 30 pairs converged cleanly (max Rhat on the interaction terms below 1.1) after up to three escalating retry rounds. The two that did not converge (Dog→Nine-banded Armadillo and Puma→Red Brocket) show no accompanying overdispersion problem, suggesting a genuine small-sample mixing difficulty at 60 spatial units rather than a misspecified model; their array-level estimates should be treated as unreliable.

Seven of 30 pairs show a credible non-zero interaction:

The 7 array-level pairs with a 95% credible interval excluding zero.
Driver Responder Source Mean Lower95 Upper95
Domestic Dog Yellow Armadillo dog_candidate -3.57 -6.54 -1.28
Domestic Dog Ocelot dog_candidate 0.64 0.00 1.35
Domestic Dog Jaguarundi dog_candidate 0.90 0.01 1.82
Ocelot Azara’s Agouti apriori 2.69 0.56 5.28
White-lipped Peccary Collared Peccary apriori 2.00 0.75 3.19
Lowland Tapir White-lipped Peccary gjam_scan 3.80 0.80 6.85
Crab-eating Fox Crab-eating Raccoon gjam_scan 2.50 0.13 5.46

Two patterns stand out. Dog abundance moves in opposite directions with different responders: negatively associated with Yellow Armadillo abundance, but positively associated with both Ocelot and Jaguarundi abundance. The armadillo result is consistent with dogs as disturbance or direct predation pressure on a slow, ground-dwelling species; the positive associations with two small cats more likely reflect shared habitat — dogs and small felids both concentrating near human-modified, easily-accessed sites — than dogs actually benefiting these predators, a distinction the model cannot resolve on its own and that would need a targeted habitat-controlled follow-up to separate. The second pattern is a clean predator-prey and facilitation cluster with no ambiguity of direction: Lowland Tapir positively predicts White-lipped Peccary abundance (both large-bodied herbivores likely tracking the same high-quality forest patches), White-lipped and Collared Peccary track each other (mixed-species peccary herding is a documented natural-history pattern), and Crab-eating Fox positively predicts Crab-eating Raccoon abundance (both generalist mesocarnivores using similar riparian and edge habitat).

4.0.1 What the interaction actually looks like

The forest plot above summarizes each pair’s strength and direction as a single coefficient with a credible interval. It is worth also seeing the underlying relationship directly: for each of the 7 significant pairs, every array’s own fitted driver abundance plotted against its own fitted responder abundance, with the model’s fitted curve overlaid.

Two pairs from the original camera-level a-priori list — Jaguar→White-lipped Peccary and Jaguar→Collared Peccary — are not shown here: at array level their point estimates keep the same negative direction seen at camera level, but the 95% credible intervals widen enough to cross zero (White-lipped Peccary: -5.17 to 2.07; Collared Peccary: -1.24 to 0.42). This is the same power-loss pattern documented throughout this module’s camera-vs-array comparison — 60 spatial replicates carry less information than several hundred cameras — and it is a real, if disappointing, consequence of the aggregation rather than an error in either fit.

A caveat on two of the seven curves. The model links the responder’s log-abundance to the driver’s raw abundance (γ0 · N_driver, not γ0 · log(N_driver)), so the effect compounds exponentially rather than linearly as driver abundance rises. Four of the 7 pairs never push the fitted responder past a plausible ceiling (500 individuals/array) anywhere in the observed range, and one more (Lowland Tapir→White-lipped Peccary) only does so for 4 of 60 arrays. For Ocelot→Azara’s Agouti and Crab-eating Fox→Crab-eating Raccoon, however, more than half the arrays (34 and 39 of 60) push the fitted responder abundance past any biologically plausible value once the driver’s own abundance climbs — a property of this particular functional form at these particular coefficient magnitudes, not a data error. The capped, log-scaled curves shown here are the right way to display that pattern; they should not be read as precise abundance predictions above roughly the observed driver range. The direction and significance of all interactions (from the actual MCMC posterior, not from this post-hoc curve) are unaffected.

4.1 The interaction network — abundance-mediated

5 GJAM: the joint species distribution model

Module 4 fits GJAM (a joint species distribution model) across all 44 species at once and reports the residual correlation between every pair — the co-occurrence left over after each species’ own habitat response has already been accounted for. Module 4 only briefly introduces GJAM since its focus is habitat, so it is worth explaining more fully here, since this module leans on it directly for the second interaction network below.

How GJAM differs from a co-occurrence occupancy model. GJAM fits one joint regression across all species simultaneously, using each species’ habitat covariates to predict its own abundance or occurrence, and then examines the covariance structure of the residuals — the part of each species’ variation that habitat does not explain. If two species’ residuals are positively correlated, they tend to be more abundant together at the same sites beyond what shared habitat alone would predict; a negative residual correlation means the opposite. This is a fundamentally different quantity from either occupancy co-occurrence or the abundance-mediated model above: GJAM never asks “does species A’s abundance drive species B’s abundance” (a directional, mechanistic claim) — it only asks “after habitat, do A and B still move together” (an undirected, purely statistical association). A GJAM residual correlation is the co-occurrence signature, not a causal interaction; it can arise from a true ecological interaction, or from a shared unmeasured covariate GJAM’s own habitat terms failed to capture, or from a shared response to a third species not in the model at all — the same omitted-variable concern flagged in the citations above, though GJAM at least explicitly controls for every measured habitat covariate before reporting the residual.

Why GJAM despite that limitation. Its value here is exactly its scale: fitting all 44 species jointly, in one model, is the only tool in this pipeline that screens the entire community for candidate co-occurrence signals in a single pass — which is precisely how the 8 GJAM-flagged pairs above were identified for a formal, directional abundance test in the first place. GJAM is the discovery instrument; the abundance-mediated model is the confirmation instrument.

5.1 The interaction network — GJAM residual co-occurrence

#> Species pairs with |r| > 0.4: 12 of 946 possible pairs

The strongest residual correlation in the whole community is Jaguarundi↔︎Southern Tiger Cat (r=0.56) — two small, ecologically similar felids whose shared positive residual likely reflects a genuine shared microhabitat preference that the 11 measured covariates do not fully capture. A cluster around Jaguarundi (also correlated with Margay, White-eared Opossum, and Crab-eating Raccoon) suggests this species sits at the center of a small-carnivore/opossum guild sharing similar habitat affinities. Separately, Capybara↔︎Puma (r=0.46) is notable given Puma is not a specialist capybara predator in this system — more likely both track riparian habitat independently.

5.2 Reading the two networks together

The abundance-mediated network answers whose abundance moves whose, on a small, hypothesis-driven set of pairs; the GJAM network answers who still co-occurs after habitat is removed, across the entire community at once, with no claim about direction or mechanism. Where the two agree, the combination is stronger evidence than either alone: Crab-eating Fox and Crab-eating Raccoon are a significant positive pair in the abundance model and one of the strongest residual correlations in the whole community (r=0.49) — two independent methods, asking different questions, converging on the same pair. Where they diverge — most pairs in the abundance model’s small hypothesis-driven list have no corresponding strong GJAM correlation, and most of GJAM’s strongest correlations (the felid/opossum cluster around Jaguarundi, the rodent pairs) were never tested directionally — the abundance model’s narrow pair list should not be read as ruling those associations out; they simply were not on this module’s shortlist of directional hypotheses to test.

6 What’s deferred to later modules

Temporal patterns — activity timing, seasonal shifts, and predator-prey timing overlap — are covered in Module 7, which picks up the interaction question from a different angle: not whether one species’ abundance affects another’s, but when each species is active relative to the others.

# What this module does

Modules 3–5 asked *where each species lives*. This module asks a harder question: **does one
species' abundance depend on another's?** That is the difference between a map of
co-occurrence and a claim about interaction — competition, predation, facilitation.

The module makes three moves:

1. **Why occupancy (co-occurrence) models are the wrong tool for inferring interactions**, and
   what the alternative is.
2. **Fit an abundance-mediated interaction model** for a focused set of driver-responder pairs,
   at the spatial resolution the data can actually support.
3. **Build two community-level interaction networks** — one from the abundance model, one from
   GJAM's residual co-occurrence — and read them together.

The most common way ecologists have tried to infer species interactions from camera-trap data

## What this means for this module
Testing all 44×43 possible species pairs with an occupancy-style co-occurrence model would be
both a multiple-testing fishing expedition and, per the above, statistically unreliable even
before the multiple-testing problem is considered. This module instead uses an
**abundance-mediated** approach — an N-mixture model where one species' *estimated abundance*

```{r fitting-summary}
#| echo: false
siv <- read_d("species_interaction_values.csv")
ppc_ok <- siv[bayes_p > .05 & bayes_p<.95 & chat<1.15, .N]
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Quantity = c("Pairs fit (a-priori)", "Pairs fit (GJAM-flagged)",
                 "Total fits (incl. reverse direction)", "Refit with ODRE",
                 "Passing posterior-predictive check"),
    Value = c(12, 8, nrow(siv), siv[used_odre==TRUE,.N], ppc_ok)),
  caption = "Camera-level fitting summary. Most pairs required the overdispersion random effect."
)
```

# GJAM: the joint species distribution model

Module 4 fits GJAM (a joint species distribution model) across all 44 species at once and
reports the **residual correlation** between every pair — the co-occurrence left over after
each species' own habitat response has already been accounted for. Module 4 only briefly
introduces GJAM since its focus is habitat, so it is worth explaining more fully here, since
this module leans on it directly for the second interaction network below.

**How GJAM differs from a co-occurrence occupancy model.** GJAM fits one joint regression
across all species simultaneously, using each species' habitat covariates to predict its own
abundance or occurrence, and then examines the **covariance structure of the residuals** — the
part of each species' variation that habitat does not explain. If two species' residuals are
positively correlated, they tend to be more abundant together at the same sites *beyond* what
shared habitat alone would predict; a negative residual correlation means the opposite. This
is a fundamentally different quantity from either occupancy co-occurrence or the
abundance-mediated model above: GJAM never asks "does species A's abundance drive species B's
abundance" (a directional, mechanistic claim) — it only asks "after habitat, do A and B still
move together" (an undirected, purely statistical association). A GJAM residual correlation
is the *co-occurrence signature*, not a causal interaction; it can arise from a true ecological

or from a shared response to a third species not in the model at all — the same

8 GJAM-flagged pairs above were identified for a formal, directional abundance test in the
first place. GJAM is the discovery instrument; the abundance-mediated model is the
confirmation instrument.

The strongest residual correlation in the whole community is Jaguarundi↔Southern Tiger Cat

guild sharing similar habitat affinities. Separately, Capybara↔Puma (r=0.46) is notable given
Puma is not a specialist capybara predator in this system — more likely both track riparian
habitat independently.

are covered in Module 7, which picks up the interaction question from a different angle: not
